name: Best pair of signals in reach
brief:
A desk logs signals as `(t, v)` pairs: the second `t` it fired and its strength `v`, which may be negative. The times strictly increase. Two signals `i < j` form a pair only when `t_j - t_i <= k`, and the pair scores `v_i + v_j + (t_j - t_i)`, since a longer gap in reach is worth more.

Write `best_signal_pair(signals, k)`, which returns the highest score of any pair, or `None` when no pair is in reach.

Example. For `signals = [(1, 3), (2, 0), (5, 10), (6, -10)]` and `k = 4`, the pair at seconds 1 and 5 scores 3 + 10 + 4 = 17, the best. The answer is 17.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 100{,}000$ signals; times are whole numbers from $0$ to $10^9$, strengths from $-10^8$ to $10^8$; $0 \le k \le 10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Checking every earlier signal in reach is too slow when `k` is large.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Rewrite the score as `(v_j + t_j) + (v_i - t_i)`. For each `j` you need the largest `v_i - t_i` among earlier signals still in reach, which is a sliding window maximum.

examples.note: Seconds 1 and 5 are 4 apart, so they are in reach and score 17.
The only two signals are 10 seconds apart, out of reach.

tests.call: best_signal_pair([(2 * i, -i) for i in range(100000)], 1000000000)

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method checks every earlier signal in reach, which is quadratic when `k` covers the whole log and runs out of time on the large tests. The step to the target is to split the score into a part for each signal and keep the best earlier part in a deque that drops signals as they leave reach.
notes: The score splits as `(v_j + t_j) + (v_i - t_i)`, so each `j` needs the largest `v_i - t_i` still in reach.
A signal leaves reach only when the gap is more than `k`; a gap of exactly `k` still counts.
The deque keeps `v - t` falling from front to back and each signal enters and leaves it once, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: Checking only neighbouring signals misses a better partner further back but still in reach.
Dropping a signal when the gap is `>= k` throws away pairs exactly `k` seconds apart.
Ranking earlier signals by strength `v` alone ignores that an older signal costs its time in the score.
